title: Block close: the voices
hook: a burning coal, a potter, dry bones, a sulking prophet, a donkey king

segments.voice: Yesterday, reading the prophets as Christians, two ways at once, and Jesus with the scroll in Nazareth. Your line was today it is fulfilled. Where did you see the promise come true, even a little? Day five hundred one.

Isaiah's lips are still stinging from a burning coal. Jeremiah, who said he was too young, has clay from the potter's house on his sleeves. Ezekiel has stood in a valley of dry bones and heard them rattle together. Daniel is fresh from the lions. Amos is still in his herdsman's clothes. Jonah is off in a corner, sulking. Hosea is talking about his children. Zechariah is describing a king on a donkey. Habakkuk argued with God and came down singing. All in one room: loud, strange, brave, often unwelcome. For weeks we've listened to them one at a time. Today, before we turn the page, we listen once more, all together.

The Hebrew word for prophet is navi, and the Bible itself shows what the job is. When Moses protests that he can't speak well, God tells him his brother Aaron will be his prophet: Aaron will say what Moses gives him to say. Not a fortune teller. A spokesperson. And look at what they spoke out about. To kings: you're not above the law. To festival crowds: your songs are noise while the poor are sold for a pair of shoes. To exiles in Babylon: comfort, you are mine, I have carved your name on my palms. To a people living in rubble: a bag with holes, and build. To the hopeless: these bones can live; your old men shall dream dreams. Two notes, over and over. Warning and comfort. Justice and hope. Here's the other thing several of them share: they pushed back on the job. Like Moses before them, some argued. Jeremiah said he was only a child. Jonah paid his fare on a ship going the other way. Amos told a priest he was no prophet, just a herdsman taken from following the flock. Isaiah does say here am I, send me, but only after a coal has touched his lips. They spoke anyway. Jeremiah said that when he tried to keep quiet, the word was like a fire shut up in his bones. Christians hear the prophets pointing forward to Jesus, the one who read their scroll in Nazareth and said today. Some also hear them pointing outward, to every place where a hard truth still needs saying. Tomorrow a new block begins: we'll read the Gospel of Luke from the very first line. And the first voices in it will sound a lot like the prophets: an old priest, a young woman, a song about the hungry filled.
screen: `A FIRE SHUT UP IN THE BONES.`
then, large: `SOMEONE HAS TO SAY IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one prophet's line to keep. Settle, and breathe. Let the lines drift past. Here am I, send me. Comfort ye my people. They shall mount up with wings as eagles. I have called thee by thy name. Let judgment run down as waters. Do justly, love mercy, walk humbly. Grace, grace unto it. Yet I will rejoice. The weeping prophet's question. Notice if one of them stays with you a little longer than the rest. Don't overthink it. Then say that one a few times, slowly, until you know it by heart. If you pray, you can offer it back to God. If you don't, simply keep it. The bell holds the time.
Navi, Hebrew for prophet, a spokesperson for God. Weeks of prophets, from Isaiah's coal to Jeremiah's balm: often reluctant messengers with two notes, warning and comfort, justice and hope.
Your line: someone has to say it. Today, keep your prophet's line close, and if a true and kind thing needs saying, say it, gently and clearly. Day five hundred one.

howItsDone: Christians read the prophets throughout the church year, especially in Advent and Lent, and many people keep a single line from them, on a card, a wall or in memory, as a word to live by.

myth: the prophets mainly predicted the future
the Bible calls Aaron Moses' prophet: his spokesperson. the prophets spoke warning and comfort to their own day, and Christians also hear them pointing to Jesus.
some prophets pushed back on their call
Jeremiah said he was only a child, and Jonah ran the other way.
the prophets spoke only words of judgment
two notes, over and over: warning and comfort, justice and hope.

fork.setup: you're Jeremiah. you've been given a hard, true word for powerful people, and you've decided not to say it. what happens?
options: you keep quiet and feel at peace.
the word burns in you until you speak.
you hand it to someone else.
fork.reveal: Jeremiah said the word was like a fire shut up in his bones; he couldn't hold it in, so he spoke.

original.note: Hebrew: prophet. in Exodus 7:1, Aaron is called Moses' prophet: the one who speaks for him.

trapdoor: what you thought: prophets were fortune tellers.
what it means: they were spokespeople, some of them reluctant, who carried two notes to their own day: warning and comfort, justice and hope.
what a scholar hears: Exodus 7:1 calls Aaron Moses' navi, the one who speaks for him: a picture of the word from inside the Bible itself.
recall: a Latin hymn from chapter one
